source.title: Observational Scaling Laws and the Predictability of Language Model Performance
source.authors: Yangjun Ruan; Chris J. Maddison; Tatsunori Hashimoto

record.file_problem: The full paper is present. Some figure text is garbled in the extraction, but the main text and the reported results used here are readable.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests whether scaling-based predictions work for downstream benchmark performance, using observational capability measures and held-out evaluations rather than the original pretraining-loss measurements.
record.gate_note: The paper discusses standard compute scaling laws and cites prior results about them, but those cited results are not rows. Its own relevant results concern downstream performance prediction. It does not measure held-out cross-entropy loss or compute-optimal parameter/token allocation.
record.test_reason: The study fits sigmoidal scaling laws for downstream benchmark, agent and prompting-method accuracy across 77 base models (plus instruction-tuned and preregistered new models) and validates them on held-out stronger models. This bears directly on V6 (downstream predictability with scale). The main predictor is benchmark-derived PC measures expressed as Llama-2-equivalent FLOPs, a surrogate for scale. Raw training-FLOPs and model-size baselines are also reported. The study measures no pretraining loss, no compute-optimal split and no architecture-shape effects.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that a low-dimensional benchmark-derived capability space lets scaling laws be built across model families. These laws accurately predict emergent tasks (as smooth sigmoids), agent performance including GPT-4, and CoT/SC gains from weaker models, whereas raw training-FLOPs fits across families predict much worse. They state the approach is for post-training analysis and does not replace compute scaling laws for pretraining. Limitations they note: contamination, within-family heterogeneity, and few-shot/basic prompting focus.
record.recipe_differences: Uses PCA-derived capability measures from standardized benchmarks, then fits sigmoid/logistic downstream-performance curves across heterogeneous model families with held-out validation; it does not fit pretraining cross-entropy power laws.
record.method_sensitivity: Prediction performance varies with the scale measure, holdout cutoff, and number of principal components. The authors report that 3 PCs generally give the most robust predictions, while lower-ranked choices can perform less well; results also vary by task.

fits_no_version.finding: Benchmark scores across 77 models are low-rank: the top 3 PCs explain about 97% of variance and PC-1 alone nearly 80%. Instruction-tuned models show about 98.6%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: LM benchmark capabilities lie in a low-dimensional space shared across model families.

record.peer_reviewed: 38th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2024)
record.problems: The study concerns downstream metrics rather than pretraining loss. The authors note possible benchmark contamination, heterogeneity within model families, and incomplete coverage of capabilities by the selected benchmarks. Some evaluations have small held-out sets; proprietary model compute information is unavailable for agent predictions.
record.rows_left_out: Not all supplementary benchmark/task curves and alternate-cutoff or alternate-PC analyses are individually recorded; the paper reports many in Figs. C.3-C.22. The primary task-specific predictions, the explicit IPA Transliterate limitation, and the principal agent and post-training outcomes are included.

untested.parts: No held-out pretraining loss vs parameters, tokens or compute is measured.
No extrapolation of pretraining loss; extrapolation is only of downstream accuracy.
No depth/width or shape variation at fixed parameter count.
No other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning or transfer scaling. Instruction-tuned models are evaluated but not trained.
Downstream performance as a function of pretraining loss is not tested.
Pretraining-loss exponents and compute-optimal splits are not fitted. Sensitivity is shown only for downstream fits (PC count, cutoff, predictor).

missing.what: Within-family log-linear relation of PC-1 (benchmark capability) to log training FLOPs, R^2 > 0.9 across families; weaker for PC-2/PC-3. This is direct evidence that downstream capability scales predictably with compute within a family.

Preregistered predictions tested on 20 new models released after May 2024, including Llama-3.1-405B. They extrapolate accurately on the emergent tasks. On GSM8K the PC MSEtest is 2.6e-03/6.0e-03/6.4e-03 vs FLOPs 8.9e-03/4.5e-02/4.6e-02.
Open LLM Leaderboard v2 tasks (GPQA, MATH Lvl 5, BBH). The observational fits give lower test MSE than FLOPs fits on harder benchmarks.
Single-family FLOPs extrapolation is accurate on one task and not the other for Qwen1.5 and OPT.
BBH with/without CoT: training-FLOPs fits give reasonable predictions (aggregation denoises) but miss Phi as an outlier.
Model-size-based fits give poor predictions of emergent tasks.
AgentBench 80/20 split underestimates held-out performance somewhat.
Holdout-cutoff sweep: PC measures have lower AUE than FLOPs/model size in 7 of 8 emergent setups.

record.verdict_notes: The PC predictor is itself derived from benchmark scores, so the support for V6 is predictability against a scale surrogate rather than against compute or loss directly. Treat the supports label with that caveat. Several figures in the extracted text are garbled; all row numbers were checked against the readable Fig. 4 labels and Table C.1.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining cross-entropy loss as a function of parameters, tokens, or compute.
Prediction of pretraining loss for much larger training runs from smaller-run loss fits.
Compute-optimal parameter and token allocation trends.
Effects of depth, width, and other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.
Scaling laws in other modalities, repeated-data training, fine-tuning, or transfer.

The study tests predictability of selected downstream benchmark and agent performance from benchmark-derived capability measures; it does not test general downstream performance as a function of pretraining loss.
Whether published pretraining-loss exponents or compute-optimal allocations vary with fitting choices, or whether pretraining-loss curves bend away from a power law.

relation.reason: Reports direct empirical tests of downstream-performance predictability, including held-out models and preregistered predictions for subsequently released models.

tranche.reason: Tests V6 using benchmark-derived capability predictors, sigmoidal downstream fits, and weaker-to-stronger holdout validation across model families.

source_check.notes: PC predictors require observed benchmark scores for target models; equivalent FLOPs are a capability transformation. The default split is 47 training and 30 held-out models; Fig. C.5 separately qualifies naive-prompting forecasts for newly released models.
